Juvenile Indo-Pacific sailfish undergo a dramatic morphological transformation during larval metamorphosis, which concludes when they reach a length of approximately 20 centimeters . This milestone marks the end of their planktonic larval appearance and the transition to a more streamlined, predatory juvenile form. Growth proceeds rapidly during the early juvenile phase, fueled by a diet of small pelagic fishes and squids. Under the thermal conditions typical of tropical surface waters (26 °C [T = 26 °C]), a female sailfish weighing around 33 kilograms can release approximately 13,150 oocytes per day , a remarkably high reproductive output that reflects the species life-history strategy. This prodigious fecundity compensates for the high rates of egg and larval mortality typical of pelagic spawning fishes, ensuring that a sufficient number of offspring survive to recruit into the adult population.

The onset of sexual maturation in Istiophorus platypterus is a gradual process, with individuals typically reaching puberty when their lower jaw-fork length attains approximately 150 centimeters [Lp = approximately 150 centimeters]. At this size, the gonads begin to develop, and vitellogenesis commences in females, preparing them for their first major spawning effort. The journey from a fertilised egg to a reproductively viable adult is energetically demanding. At the very start of this journey, the wet weight at birth, based on an egg diameter of 1.3 millimeters, is a mere 0.0012 grams [Wwb = 0.0012 grams]. This negligible initial mass highlights the extreme vulnerability of the early life stages, which must quickly find suitable prey and avoid a vast array of predators in the open ocean to survive the initial weeks of exogenous feeding.

As sailfish continue to grow beyond puberty, they can achieve truly impressive ultimate sizes. The maximum recorded lower jaw-fork length for this species is approximately 348 centimeters [Li = approximately 348 centimeters], a formidable dimension that places it among the largest of the billfishes. Correspondingly, the ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult can reach up to 100,000 grams [Wwi = up to 100,000 grams], a mass that supports their high-speed predatory lifestyle. Individuals of this size are apex predators in the pelagic ecosystem, capable of incredible bursts of speed to capture tuna and mackerel. The attainment of such a large body size is a slow process, tempered by the energetic costs of maintaining a high-performance physiology in warm waters.

The life span of the Indo-Pacific sailfish, when living in waters consistently around 26 °C [T = 26 °C], has been estimated at approximately 13 years [am = approximately 13 years]. This longevity is notable for a fast-growing, highly active pelagic predator and allows for multiple spawning seasons over an individuals lifetime. The species is iteroparous, spawning several times throughout the year when conditions are favorable. The trade-off between rapid juvenile growth and extended adult lifespan is a central theme in the species life history; the initial high mortality is offset by a long reproductive window, during which the billions of eggs produced annually by a single female can contribute significantly to the next generation.

From a comparative physiological perspective, the sailfish growth trajectory underscores a fascinating pattern of investment. The jump from a birth weight of 0.0012 grams [Wwb = 0.0012 grams] to an adult weight of 100,000 grams [Wwi = 100,000 grams] represents an increase of eight orders of magnitude in body mass, with much of this growth achieved after the juvenile stage. The transition through puberty at a fork length of approximately 150 centimeters [Lp = approximately 150 centimeters] marks a pivotal shift in energy allocation towards gamete production. Interestingly, the reported daily reproductive rate of approximately 13,150 eggs per day  at a body weight of 33 kilograms, measured at 26 °C, highlights an exceptionally high metabolic and energetic throughput for a fish of that size, which is consistent with the elevated metabolic demands of being an active, warm-bodied predator at a temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C].
